title: RDF 1.1 Semantics assertion inventory
method: AI close reading of the complete substantive specification, following its definitions, quantifiers, tables, theorems and document structure; HTML structure was used to verify anchors, not to extract obligations by keyword.

taxonomy.definition: Introduces an entity, notation, structure, relation, operation or inherited abstract-syntax concept.
taxonomy.semantic_constraint: Restricts interpretations, denotations or truth values; includes axiomatic triple families.
taxonomy.general_requirement: Specifies scope, conformance, permissions, recommendations, extension requirements or limits on what follows operationally.
taxonomy.mathematical_consequence: States a theorem, derived entailment, non-entailment, equivalence, complexity result or explicitly identified consequence inferred during this reading.

field_conventions.source_status: Normative or informative status of the cited source passage, not a command to implement an algorithm. Examples and notes remain informative even inside normative sections.
field_conventions.assertion_basis: explicit means stated by the source; incorporated means imported through a source reference; derived means the inventory author inferred it and it is not a separately stated source requirement.
field_conventions.official_rule_code: Only published rule identifiers are populated. Local record IDs and source HTML condition IDs are not official entailment rules.
field_conventions.source_locator: Disambiguates components or conjuncts sharing a source anchor; the five numbered simple-interpretation components retain their original numbers.
field_conventions.dependencies: Selected local conceptual dependencies, not a certified minimal proof dependency graph.
field_conventions.assessment: Every implementation mapping, proof obligation and test mapping is unassessed; an inventory entry is not evidence of conformance.

coverage_notes.reading: All substantive sections 1–10 and informative appendices A–D were read; the document structure and normative/informative boundaries were checked. Concepts is included only where needed by this document.
coverage_notes.completeness: Reading a section does not establish that every independent assertion has been inventoried. This is a reviewable first pass, not an exhaustive formalization or certified completeness result.
coverage_notes.granularity: Semantic conditions and published rule patterns are split. Uniform axiomatic triple families are grouped with explicit members or a quantified schema. Repeated theorems in Appendix C are attached as supporting references rather than duplicated.
coverage_notes.tests: W3C rdf-tests are important independent conformance evidence, not an exhaustive catalogue of normative obligations or a proof of coverage. No test-to-record mapping is asserted here.
coverage_notes.scope: RDF 1.1 Semantics is primary; graph sethood and other abstract-syntax definitions imported from Concepts are included. No RDF 1.2, SPARQL bag semantics or repository-specific query API contract is imported implicitly.
exclusions: Administrative front matter, change history, acknowledgements and bibliography metadata are not independent implementation obligations.
Worked examples and diagrams are generally evidence for an assertion rather than separate records; illustrative counterexamples are summarized when they distinguish regimes.
Appendix C proof steps are not individually inventoried; theorem assumptions and supporting proof locations are retained.
Externally defined datatype lexical spaces, XML canonicalization algorithms and all RFC grammar productions are referenced dependencies, not recursively expanded here.
No claim is made to enumerate all logical consequences of the normative semantics.

This first-pass inventory is not itself proof or implementation evidence. Current Lean mappings and checks are recorded separately in the cleanroom catalogue; implementation refinement and test-to-record mapping remain open.
coverage_notes.source_ambiguities: Potential contradictions or omitted assumptions are review questions. The pinned text is preserved separately from a proposed mathematical reading; none is labelled confirmed W3C errata.
coverage_notes.character_traceability: The historical first-pass inventory carries section anchors. The separate cleanroom catalogue now binds selected passages to hash-pinned source bytes and Unicode scalar ranges, with unresolved intervals and pending expert review explicit.
remaining_inventory_review: Review grouped prose assertions and example-derived scope limitations for any further useful splitting.
Expand imported Concepts definitions and external datatype specifications only as needed by the chosen formalization scope.
Resolve the recorded source questions before adopting the affected claims as trusted formal statements.
Review intended-use statements in Appendix D separately from the normative model-theoretic constraints.

review_questions.question: The final paragraph says recognizing more datatypes strengthens entailment but states E-entailment implies D-entailment when D is a subset of E, and D-entailment implies simple entailment. Compare these directions against the universal-model definition and section 3 monotonic-extension requirement.
review_questions.mathematical_comparison: Under compatible fixed datatype meanings, every E-interpretation is a D-interpretation, so truth preservation over all D-models implies truth preservation over all E-models. Empty-D entailment is simple entailment.

review_questions.question: Section 9.2 states that RDFS entailment implies RDF entailment because every RDFS interpretation is an RDF interpretation, while also claiming RDFS entailment is stronger. Compare the quantified model classes.
review_questions.mathematical_comparison: For the same D, RDFS models form a subclass of RDF models; RDF entailment therefore implies RDFS entailment. The reverse does not follow from subclass inclusion.

review_questions.question: The table of additional rdfs-valid triples includes rdf:XMLLiteral and rdf:HTML as rdfs:Class without an explicit recognition premise; section 8 permits these datatype IRIs to be unrecognized. Establish the intended premise or derivation before treating these entries as unconditional theorems.

Appendix A calls closures finite after speaking of RDF graphs generally, while section 5.3 permits infinite graphs. Determine and document the finite/effective-input restriction required by the finiteness and complexity assertions.
review_questions.mathematical_comparison: The closure contains its premise S, so it cannot be finite when S is infinite.

review_questions.question: The printed conclusion has only an existential blank subject and can reuse the premise metadata witness. Is the intended claim instead about two fixed distinct reification resources or another explicit scope?
review_questions.mathematical_comparison: ReificationScopeReview.printed_conclusion_follows proves the positive simple entailment of the exact graph shape.

records.paraphrase: The specification assigns model-theoretic truth conditions to RDF graphs and RDF/RDFS vocabularies, characterizing truth-preserving transformations and derivations.
Passages are normative except sections explicitly marked non-normative and authoring guidelines, diagrams, examples and notes.
Capitalized requirement keywords have their RFC 2119 meanings.
Normative authority concerns RDF semantics and inference validity; social naming conventions and relationships to non-RDF Web content are outside the specified semantics.
Additional semantic assumptions about an RDF vocabulary constitute a semantic extension and determine an entailment regime.
Extensions may restrict legal graph syntax and treat violations as errors; none of the extensions normatively defined here adds such graph restrictions.
Whenever G simply entails H, every extension must preserve that entailment if its additional syntactic conditions hold; stronger semantics cannot cancel an accepted simple entailment.
IRI, triple, graph, subject, predicate, object, RDF source, node, blank node, literal, graph isomorphism and dataset have their Concepts meanings.
An RDF graph is a set of RDF triples, using RDF-term identity for its triple components.
records.formalization_note: A list implementation may represent a graph through its membership set; this definition alone does not establish a unique enumeration or a correct cardinality operation.

records.paraphrase: An ordinary RDF triple has an IRI or blank-node subject, an IRI predicate, and an IRI, blank-node or literal object; those term kinds are distinct.
Abstract IRI and literal identity follow Concepts, not equality of denoted values; blank-node identifiers are concrete-syntax labels rather than the abstract blank nodes themselves.
records.formalization_note: Check literal language-tag identity against Concepts separately from the lowercase language-tag value condition in section 7.1.

records.paraphrase: All definitions apply unchanged to generalized triples, graphs and datasets, whose triple positions can each contain any RDF term.
An interpretation maps IRIs and literals into a semantic domain subject to constraints; qualified kinds of interpretation determine corresponding entailment regimes.

Denoting and referring name the interpretation-dependent relationship to a referent; identifying denotes an externally established naming relationship, which need not agree with a particular interpretation.
Equality denotes strict identity, and angle-bracket pairs are ordered pairs; these conventions apply throughout the mathematics.
A name is an IRI or literal; a typed literal contributes itself and its datatype IRI as names, and a vocabulary is a set of names.
The empty graph is the empty set of triples.
Subgraphs and proper subgraphs are respectively subsets and proper subsets of triples; a triple is identified with its singleton subgraph.
A ground graph has no blank nodes.
An instance is obtained by consistently replacing some or all blank nodes through a function into RDF terms; names already in the graph are unchanged.
Instantiation is reflexive and composes transitively; every resulting triple is an instance of at least one original triple.
An instance relative to vocabulary V uses only names in V for substituted names; substitutions by blank nodes are still permitted.
An instance is proper if some blank node becomes a name or distinct blank nodes are identified by the substitution.
Graph isomorphism is an invertible renaming of blank nodes, leaving names fixed; isomorphic graphs are mutual instances and may be treated as identical up to that renaming.
A graph is lean if none of its instances is a proper subgraph of itself.
A non-lean graph is logically redundant relative to its lean subgraphs; every ground graph is lean.
Repeated occurrences of the identical triple do not add graph members, and order does not distinguish graphs with the same members.
records.formalization_note: This is the mathematical consequence of sethood, not a separately coded entailment rule or a requirement to reject duplicate surface-syntax statements.

records.paraphrase: Blank-node sharing between graphs requires a source structure that provides for shared identity; repeated retrieval of the same document or source does not by itself identify its blank nodes.
Applications manipulating scoped blank-node labels should track the abstract identities and rename labels when combining sources to prevent accidental conflation.
records.formalization_note: This is an authoring/implementation guideline under the section 2 exception, not a new truth condition.

records.paraphrase: Graph union uses triple-set union and preserves actual blank-node identities, including identities shared across inputs.
Merge first separates blank nodes shared between inputs, then takes their union; merging subgraphs can therefore produce a larger graph.
The union is an instance of the merge; when inputs share no blank nodes, union and merge coincide. Union retains the joint content, including shared blank-node meaning.
All semantic extensions must preserve the simple truth conditions; they may add constraints but must not modify or negate those conditions.
Semantics applies to a graph rather than a changing RDF source; a source is interpreted through its graph value at a time or state, while a fixed graph does not change meaning with time.
A simple interpretation includes a nonempty resource set IR.
records.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 1

records.paraphrase: A simple interpretation includes a property set IP.
records.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 2

records.paraphrase: IEXT maps each element of IP to a subset of IR × IR; this set of pairs is the property extension.
records.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 3

records.paraphrase: IS maps every IRI into IR ∪ IP.
records.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 4
records.formalization_note: There is no injectivity or unique-names requirement; different IRIs may denote the same object.

records.paraphrase: IL is a partial function from literals into IR; a literal may have no denotation.
records.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 5

records.paraphrase: A literal evaluates using IL and an IRI using IS.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, first and second rows

records.paraphrase: A ground triple is true precisely when its predicate denotes a member of IP and its subject/object denotations form a pair in that property extension; otherwise it is false.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, third row

records.paraphrase: A ground graph is true exactly when every member triple is true; one false member makes it false.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, fourth row

records.paraphrase: A triple containing a literal with undefined IL is false, and a graph containing that triple is false.
The empty graph is true under every simple interpretation and remains true under conforming semantic extensions wherever their syntax admits it.
IP and IR may overlap. In a true triple subject/object denotations lie in IR; an IRI used as both predicate and subject/object in a true graph denotes an element of IP ∩ IR.
records.formalization_note: The dual-role conclusion requires satisfaction of the relevant graph/triples; a false occurrence alone supplies no membership constraint.

records.paraphrase: An extension may constrain particular IRI denotations, including fixing denotations of recognized datatype IRIs.
For an assignment A from blank nodes to IR, I+A agrees with I on names and with A on its blank-node domain; triple and graph evaluation then uses the ground rules.
A graph is true under I exactly when there exists one assignment of all its blank nodes to IR that makes the entire graph true.
records.formalization_note: The existential assignment has whole-graph scope and must be consistent across every occurrence of each blank node; per-triple independent assignments would weaken the condition.

records.paraphrase: Blank-node assignments are witnesses to graph truth rather than components of I; blank nodes have no globally fixed denotation under a simple interpretation.
Evaluating a list through its set of triples gives the same satisfaction result after permuting or repeating identical triples, while preserving blank-node identity.
records.formalization_note: This proves a possible set abstraction, not that list length, duplicate-returning scans, or repository APIs refine graph cardinality or unique enumeration.

records.paraphrase: Separately satisfying graphs that share a blank node need not satisfy their union; union requires a common witness across those occurrences and changes existential scope.
I satisfies E when E evaluates to true; E is satisfiable if some simple interpretation satisfies it and unsatisfiable if none does.
G simply entails E when every simple interpretation satisfying G also satisfies E.
records.formalization_note: The universal interpretation is shared by premise and conclusion, but their existential blank-node witness assignments need not be the same; joint graph meaning requires union when sharing matters.

records.paraphrase: Graphs are logically equivalent exactly when each entails the other.
The document does not independently define entailment from a set of graphs; first form a union or merge, choosing whether shared blank-node identities must be retained.
A graph-producing process is simply valid if every output is simply entailed by its corresponding input, and invalid otherwise.

Semantic validity does not require an application to execute an inference, and invalidity does not prohibit a transformation; the specification characterizes truth preservation rather than mandating graph operations.
Entailment preserves truth, not application-specific suitability; properties such as being a usable test manifest need not survive valid entailment.
Every RDF graph has a satisfying simple interpretation; this assertion does not extend automatically to datatype-aware regimes.
G simply entails E exactly when an instance of E is a subgraph of G.

Simple entailment is decidable for finite input graphs by searching for a substitution whose image is a subset of the premise; the general problem is computationally hard, while a ground conclusion reduces to subset checking.
records.formalization_note: The text permits infinite graphs elsewhere; an algorithmic decidability claim requires finite effective input. Appendix A states NP-completeness explicitly.

records.paraphrase: Every graph simply entails the empty graph, and the empty graph simply entails only itself.
Every graph simply entails each of its subgraphs.
Every instance of a graph simply entails that graph.
A lean graph does not simply entail a proper instance of itself.
records.formalization_note: The source states the consequence without finiteness. The checked theorem assumes finite occurring blank support, which finite graphs satisfy. Under LeanGraph, the unrestricted consequence is equivalent to absence of a proper self-instance. An infinite ordinary self-instance example is proved non-lean and is not a counterexample to the source theorem. The missing unrestricted self-instance exclusion remains open.

records.paraphrase: If S is a subgraph of S-prime and S simply entails E, then S-prime simply entails E.
If S simply entails a finite E, some finite subset of S already entails E; S itself may be infinite.
records.formalization_note: Do not replace RDF graph sethood by finiteness without recording the restriction.

records.paraphrase: A graph cannot simply entail a graph containing an IRI absent from the premise.
Skolemization replaces blank nodes consistently with fresh IRIs coined for this purpose, with distinct blank nodes receiving distinct fresh IRIs.
records.formalization_note: Freshness is relative to other graphs at creation; the injectivity requirement is explicit in the Appendix C proof.

records.paraphrase: A skolemized graph simply entails its original graph.
A graph with at least one blank node does not simply entail its skolemization, because the latter introduces a fresh IRI.
records.formalization_note: The nonempty-blank premise is explicitly supplied by the preceding §6 paragraph beginning Suppose G is a graph containing blank nodes. For a ground graph the transformation is identity; the displayed non-entailment must retain its surrounding scope.

records.paraphrase: If sk(G) simply entails H, there is H-prime with G entailing H-prime and H = sk(H-prime), using the corresponding inverse replacement of skolem IRIs.
records.formalization_note: Exact ordinary lifting is proved using separate copies of source and conclusion blanks. Reapplication extends the original naming map on the source copy and preserves conclusion blanks; it is not the existing ambient-total substitution. The source's implicit blank-scope convention and Appendix C commutation explanation remain expert-review questions. Generalized semantic lifting is also proved directly through interpretations.

records.paraphrase: For H containing none of the freshly introduced skolem IRIs, sk(G) simply entails H exactly when G simply entails H.
D is the set of datatype IRIs recognized by an interpretation; recognizing an IRI presupposes determining the unique datatype it identifies.
A recognized datatype IRI identifies the same externally specified datatype at every occurrence; the mechanism establishing that identification is outside this semantics.
The datatype map associated with D is the interpretation restricted to D; descriptions parameterized by a datatype map can use this fixed map.
records.formalization_note: This definition occurs inside a change note and is therefore informative under section 2.

records.paraphrase: Literal structure and datatype definitions come from Concepts: ordinary datatype literals pair a lexical string with a datatype IRI; language-tagged strings additionally use a language tag and rdf:langString.
A datatype supplies a lexical space and a partial lexical-to-value mapping; L2V selects that mapping and its range is the value space.
A literal is ill-typed relative to D when its datatype IRI is recognized but its lexical form has no value under the corresponding mapping.
RDF processors need not recognize datatype IRIs beyond rdf:langString and xsd:string; recognizing additional IRIs is permitted.
records.formalization_note: The minimum is imposed on RDF interpretations in section 8, not on arbitrary simple D-interpretations, where D can be empty.

records.paraphrase: If a datatype IRI listed in Concepts section 5 is recognized, its specified meaning must be used; recognition of rdf:PlainLiteral requires its separately specified meaning.
When another datatype IRI is recognized, its identification must be unambiguous and remain fixed throughout RDF transformations and manipulations.
rdf:langString identifies a datatype whose values are string/language-tag pairs, with specially defined literal interpretation instead of an L2V mapping.
A literal with an unrecognized datatype IRI should not be rejected solely for that reason and should be treated as denoting some resource like an unknown name; warnings are permitted.
records.formalization_note: Unknown datatype and recognized datatype with invalid lexical form are different cases. Preserve the SHOULD and MAY force of these statements.

records.paraphrase: A D-interpretation is a simple interpretation satisfying the additional datatype conditions for its recognized set D.
If rdf:langString belongs to D, each language-tagged literal denotes its lexical string paired with its language tag converted to lowercase by US-ASCII rules.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, first row

records.paraphrase: For each other IRI in D, its interpretation is the datatype it identifies.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, second row, datatype-denotation conjunct

records.paraphrase: For a literal typed with a recognized IRI other than rdf:langString, IL is the corresponding lexical-to-value result, including being undefined when that mapping is undefined.
records.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, second row, literal-value conjunct

records.paraphrase: Every graph containing an ill-typed literal is false in every D-interpretation; unrecognized datatype IRIs do not create this source of D-unsatisfiability.
Syntactically legal rdf:langString literals always denote when recognized. For xsd:string, the source limits ill-typed forms to strings containing code points outside the XML Char production.
records.formalization_note: The xsd:string character-domain constraint needs explicit modeling; do not infer that every host-language string is a valid xsd:string value.

records.paraphrase: D-satisfiability means having at least one satisfying D-interpretation; S D-entails G when every D-interpretation satisfying S also satisfies G.
A graph can lack any satisfying D-interpretation; processors may report this as an error but are not required to do so.
A D-unsatisfiable graph D-entails every graph by the universal-model definition.
records.formalization_note: This is a vacuous implication over no satisfying models, not an inconsistent interpretation admitted into the model class.

records.paraphrase: The ex-falso consequence is not an instruction or authorization to produce arbitrary application conclusions from inconsistent data.
With D empty, D-entailment is exactly simple entailment.
The final paragraph states that E-entailment implies D-entailment for D contained in E, and that D-entailment implies simple entailment, while saying more recognized datatypes strengthen entailment.
records.formalization_note: Recorded as a source claim awaiting review; do not translate it into a trusted theorem without resolving the direction.

records.paraphrase: With compatible fixed datatype meanings and D contained in E, every E-interpretation is a D-interpretation; therefore D-entailment implies E-entailment, and simple entailment implies D-entailment.
Literals recognized to have the same value can be substituted in corresponding triples to obtain datatype entailments, including across different recognized datatypes with overlapping value spaces.
A fixed generic syntactic pattern set does not capture all datatype entailments; the actual lexical-to-value mappings can supply additional consequences.
Ill-typed literals are the only source of unsatisfiability for simple D-entailment; adding RDF/RDFS vocabulary conditions can introduce other sources.
An RDF interpretation recognizing D is a D-interpretation in which D includes rdf:langString and xsd:string and the RDF conditions and axiomatic triples hold.
x belongs to IP exactly when the pair of x and the denotation of rdf:Property belongs to the extension of rdf:type.
records.source_locator: RDF semantic condition with HTML identifier rdfsemcond1

records.paraphrase: For each datatype IRI a in D, rdf:type relates x to I(a) exactly when x belongs to that datatype value space.
records.source_locator: RDF semantic condition with HTML identifier rdfsemcond3; the source has no rdfsemcond2 row

records.paraphrase: Each listed RDF vocabulary IRI must satisfy its rdf:type rdf:Property axiomatic triple.
The triple rdf:nil rdf:type rdf:List is true in every RDF interpretation.
For every positive integer n, rdf:_n rdf:type rdf:Property is an RDF axiom.
records.formalization_note: This is an infinite indexed family; a finite implementation vocabulary needs a justified restriction.

records.paraphrase: No other special normative meanings are imposed on the remaining RDF vocabulary; recognizing rdf:XMLLiteral and rdf:HTML is optional.

S RDF-entails E recognizing D when every satisfying RDF interpretation of S recognizing D satisfies E; an RDF-unsatisfiable graph has no such model. Unqualified RDF entailment uses D = {rdf:langString, xsd:string}.
The empty graph RDF-entails every RDF axiom, so the simple-entailment interpolation characterization does not extend unchanged to RDF entailment.
From a triple s p literal typed with d in D, infer a graph containing s p b and b rdf:type d for one existential blank node b.
records.formalization_note: Both conclusion triples use the same witness; the pattern remains semantically valid for an ill-typed premise through unsatisfiability.

records.paraphrase: From s p o, RDF-entail p rdf:type rdf:Property.
Datatype value spaces can force entailments beyond rdfD1/rdfD2, and incompatible memberships in disjoint recognized datatype value spaces can make a graph RDF-unsatisfiable.
records.formalization_note: The boolean example uses exhaustiveness of the two boolean values; it cannot be obtained from lexical-value equality alone.

records.paraphrase: Classes are resources typed rdfs:Class; IC collects them, and ICEXT maps classes to subsets of IR. Distinct classes can share an extension.
records.formalization_note: Empty-extension permission is split into MT11-RDFS-EMPTY-CLASS-PERMITTED. The same source paragraph also states universal rdfs:Class self-membership, connected to the additional-valid-types proof rather than only a permitted-model example.

records.paraphrase: An RDFS class may have an empty class extension.
records.formalization_note: A constructed RDFS model has an unnamed class whose ICEXT is exactly empty. This is an existence witness under the existing sufficient constructor Parameters, not a requirement that every model contain an empty class or that every class can be empty.

records.paraphrase: An RDFS interpretation recognizing D is an RDF interpretation recognizing the same D that satisfies the RDFS semantic conditions and axiomatic triples.
ICEXT(y) is the set of x such that rdf:type relates x to y.
IC is ICEXT of the denotation of rdfs:Class.
LV is ICEXT of the denotation of rdfs:Literal.
The extension of rdfs:Resource is exactly IR.
The extension of rdf:langString is exactly the set of denotations of language-tagged literals.
For every other datatype IRI a in D, ICEXT(I(a)) is its value space.
Every recognized datatype denotation belongs to the extension of rdfs:Datatype.
If rdfs:domain relates property x to class y and x relates u to v, then u belongs to ICEXT(y).
If rdfs:range relates property x to class y and x relates u to v, then v belongs to ICEXT(y).
The extension of rdfs:subPropertyOf is transitive on IP.
Every property in IP is related to itself by rdfs:subPropertyOf.
Both endpoints of any rdfs:subPropertyOf pair belong to IP.
If rdfs:subPropertyOf relates x to y, IEXT(x) is a subset of IEXT(y).
records.formalization_note: The converse is not required; extension inclusion alone does not force a subproperty assertion.

records.paraphrase: Every class in IC is related to rdfs:Resource by rdfs:subClassOf.
The extension of rdfs:subClassOf is transitive on IC.
Every class in IC is related to itself by rdfs:subClassOf.
Both endpoints of any rdfs:subClassOf pair belong to IC.
records.source_locator: rdfssemcond7, endpoint-typing conjunct; source order places condition 8 before condition 7

records.paraphrase: If rdfs:subClassOf relates x to y, ICEXT(x) is a subset of ICEXT(y).
records.formalization_note: The converse is not required; equal or included class extensions do not by themselves force subclass assertions.

records.paraphrase: Every member of the rdfs:ContainerMembershipProperty class is a subproperty of rdfs:member.
Every member of the rdfs:Datatype class is a subclass of rdfs:Literal.
Every property/class pair in this family is an axiomatic rdfs:domain triple.
Every property/class pair in this family is an axiomatic rdfs:range triple.
The listed vocabulary hierarchy triples are true in every RDFS interpretation.
For every positive integer n, rdf:_n has type rdfs:ContainerMembershipProperty, domain rdfs:Resource, and range rdfs:Resource.
records.formalization_note: One uniformly indexed family containing the three corresponding axiom schemas; no finite maximum n is imposed.

records.paraphrase: IP equals ICEXT(I(rdf:Property)); recognized datatypes act as classes with their value-space extensions, and recognized literals either lack denotation or denote members of those classes.
The source lists these additional rdfs:Class typings as valid in all RDFS interpretations; it explicitly does not claim the list is complete.
records.formalization_note: Twelve core class entries are derived from existing axioms and rules. The separate recognized-datatype theorem covers XMLLiteral/HTML only with a D-recognition premise. Their printed unqualified validity remains an open source question. The list is explicitly non-exhaustive.

records.paraphrase: The source lists these additional rdf:Property typings as valid in all RDFS interpretations.

Resources, classes and properties are not disjoint categories; class self-membership and property self-application are allowed, while properties of a class do not automatically transfer to its members or conversely.

The meanings of rdfs:comment, rdfs:seeAlso, rdfs:isDefinedBy and rdfs:label are constrained only through their specified domain/range/subproperty uses. The axiom/condition set intentionally contains redundancy.
records.formalization_note: The inventory does not require redundant source assertions to become independent implementation mechanisms.

records.paraphrase: rdfs:Literal classifies literal values rather than literal syntax; an IRI or blank node may denote such a value, so IRI subjects typed rdfs:Literal can be consistent.
S RDFS-entails E recognizing D when every RDFS interpretation recognizing D that satisfies S also satisfies E.
The source states that RDFS entailment implies RDF entailment because RDFS interpretations are RDF interpretations, while also saying RDFS entailment is stronger.

For the same D, RDF entailment implies RDFS entailment by restricting the universal quantifier to the RDFS interpretations; the source also identifies IRI rdf:type rdfs:Resource triples as RDFS-valid.
records.formalization_note: The general model-class direction is author-derived; the resource-typing family is explicitly stated as an example in the source.

records.paraphrase: For every recognized datatype IRI d in D, entail d rdf:type rdfs:Datatype.
records.formalization_note: Pattern variables denote RDF terms; repeated variables agree across all premises and conclusions. Generalized syntax is needed when instantiation places a literal in subject position or a blank node in predicate position. The letter D in class-pattern variables is not the recognized-datatype-set parameter.

Generalized syntax is needed when instantiation places a literal in subject position or a blank node in predicate position. The letter D in class-pattern variables is not the recognized-datatype-set parameter.

Generalized syntax is needed when instantiation places a literal in subject position or a blank node in predicate position. records.paraphrase: RDFS domain or range consequences can force an individual into disjoint recognized datatype classes and thereby make a graph unsatisfiable.
A dataset has one default graph and zero or more named graphs under the Concepts definition; component graphs may share blank nodes.
A graph name used as an RDF term need not denote its associated graph, and engines should not presume that relationship without an external reason.
A dataset may be used to express RDF content; when it is, it should carry at least the semantic content of its default graph.
records.formalization_note: MAY and SHOULD do not define a complete, uniquely mandated dataset entailment relation.

records.paraphrase: Replacing the default graph by a logically equivalent graph need not preserve dataset structure or cross-graph blank-node sharing.
records.formalization_note: The paragraph starts with an ordinary prose caution, not a styled note; structural isomorphism and logical equivalence remain distinct.

records.paraphrase: Semantic extensions may impose further dataset meaning and restrictions; comparing corresponding named graphs is an example rather than the required core semantics.
The ordinary rule-based check augments the premise with relevant axioms, saturates it with inference patterns, then tests whether some instance of the conclusion is included.
records.formalization_note: The appendix is informative; this procedure is not a mandatory implementation architecture.

procedure_steps.operation: Add all RDF or RDF+RDFS axiomatic triples that do not contain container membership IRIs.
Add axioms containing each container membership IRI that occurs in the conclusion.
Apply the appropriate RDF/RDFS inference patterns until no new triples are produced.
Check whether the enlarged graph contains an instance of the conclusion.

records.paraphrase: A positive result from the ordinary-syntax procedure establishes entailment, but some valid RDF/RDFS entailments are missed.
records.formalization_note: The examples expose shared datatype witnesses and intermediate blank-node predicates; implementing every displayed rule on legal RDF triples alone does not establish completeness.

records.paraphrase: For a premise triple containing a literal typed by d in D, infer the generalized triple literal rdf:type d.

The generalized RDF/RDFS closure of S towards E adds the prescribed finite-vocabulary axioms and saturates generalized triples with GrdfD1, rdfD2 and, for RDFS, rdfs1–rdfs13 at the base recognized datatype set.

procedure_steps.operation: Add RDF or RDF+RDFS axioms not containing a container membership IRI.
For every container membership IRI in E, add the axioms containing it.
If step 2 added no triples, add the axioms containing rdf:_1.
Saturate under GrdfD1 and rdfD2, plus rdfs1–rdfs13 for RDFS, with D = {rdf:langString, xsd:string}.

records.paraphrase: If S is RDF-consistent, respectively RDFS-consistent, then S entails E in that regime exactly when the corresponding generalized closure towards E simply entails E.
records.formalization_note: Retain the consistency premise, regime-specific closure and base datatype set. This theorem does not automatically cover arbitrary additional datatypes or inconsistent inputs.

records.paraphrase: For finite effective input, the generalized closure is finite and its generation is decidable with polynomial complexity.
records.formalization_note: The source states finite closures without restating a finite-input premise; an infinite S cannot have a finite closure containing it. This is a scope question, not a confirmed erratum.

records.paraphrase: Simple entailment is NP-complete in general for finite inputs, while a conclusion without blank nodes admits a low-order polynomial check.
records.formalization_note: Keep the complexity of closure generation separate from the subsequent existential substitution search.

records.paraphrase: A practical subset of the rules can miss consequences; replacing GrdfD1 with legal-syntax rdfD1 also loses completeness. Larger recognized datatype sets require datatype-specific reasoning.
A pre-interpretation uses a restricted vocabulary V and maps only names in that vocabulary, enabling smaller semantic structures for the graphs being compared.
records.formalization_note: The precise refinement reuses normative section 5 on the two vocabulary subtypes: IS maps into IR union IP and IL remains partial. Appendix B informally describes a mapping into IR; the formalization choice is explicit and awaiting expert review.

records.paraphrase: The sketch restricts to the names in G union E and gives a resource bound N+B+1, where N counts names and B counts blank nodes, with extensions preserving relevant triple truth values.
records.formalization_note: Under the explicit section-5-faithful refinement of pre-interpretations, the N+B+1 bound is proved for the entire active domain IR union IP and hence for IR. B counts distinct blank identities in the union, and N counts names including literal datatype IRIs. Bounded-preinterpretation entailment and satisfiability equivalences are proved. Domain compression preserves a chosen premise witness and reflects conclusion truth; subsequent name completion preserves all truth over V. This does not establish D/RDF/RDFS bounds or an executable decision procedure.

records.paraphrase: The simple pre-interpretations considered in Appendix B admit full-name completions preserving relevant truth; restricting name domains does not change satisfiability or entailment for graphs over those names.
records.formalization_note: This isolates name-domain completion and locality from the separate finite-resource bound. The precise construction retains normative section 5 typing and partial IL. The entailment equivalence quantifies over all V-preinterpretations, not only finite carriers.

records.paraphrase: For datatype entailment, the sketch weakens value requirements to literals occurring in the compared graphs and gives the bound (N+B)×(D+1), with D here counting recognized datatypes.
records.formalization_note: Localized datatype conditions now admit an N+B+1 active-domain compression, a full-to-weakened countermodel theorem and bounded satisfiability equivalence. This is partial evidence for the printed (N+B)*(D+1) claim, not that formula or entailment equivalence. For empty G and E the printed bound is zero for every finite datatype count, incompatible with the section-5 nonempty-IR refinement; an explicit theorem records this boundary and empty-graph D-satisfiability. No source correction is adopted. The numerical D must be distinguished from the recognized-IRI set; counting aliases and datatype identities is an external scope question. A separate completion proof now gives bounded-pre-model entailment equivalence for ordinary conclusions; the generalized conclusion case has a checked scope obstruction under the chosen weakening.

records.paraphrase: For RDF/RDFS, the sketch restricts container vocabulary and relevant literal values, and claims suitable finite pre-interpretations extend to full interpretations without changing truth or entailment for the compared graphs.
records.formalization_note: Do not replace global datatype value-space conditions by finite observed values without the stated extension/preservation argument.

records.paraphrase: Appendix C supplies proof arguments for the previously stated empty-graph, subgraph, instance, satisfiability, interpolation, lean-instance, fresh-IRI and skolemization results.
records.formalization_note: These theorem records carry supporting proof links; individual proof steps are outside this first inventory. A proof in the source is not an assessed Lean proof.

records.paraphrase: Much reification, container and collection intent is deliberately omitted from the formal semantic conditions; the appendix discusses intended use rather than adding mandatory entailments.
Reification uses rdf:Statement, rdf:subject, rdf:predicate and rdf:object to describe an RDF triple token or concrete realization.
Reification relates a triple token to the resources its components denote, rather than quoting the component IRIs as syntactic objects.
Reifying a triple does not entail asserting it, and asserting a triple does not entail the existence of its reification.
Multiple reifications can describe matching components without denoting the same token; properties asserted of one such entity need not transfer to another.
Container vocabulary describes entities with a type and partial membership information; indexed membership properties distinguish positions, while rdfs:member is generic membership.

The informal intended uses are an unordered duplicate-permitting bag, an ordered sequence, and alternatives that may have a preference order; indexed properties are intended as single-valued positions.
records.formalization_note: These intended properties are not additional formal RDF entailment conditions. Permitting duplicate bag members is not permitting repeated identical triples in an RDF graph.

records.paraphrase: The bag interpretation does not justify permuting indexed membership assertions as an RDF entailment.
A property of a container does not automatically hold of its members, nor does a member property automatically hold of the container.
Formal semantics does not require container classes to be disjoint or indexed positions to be gap-free.
records.formalization_note: Gap and overlapping-type witnesses are separate from the three membership-count, extension-consistency and finiteness obligations split from paragraph 15 into their own records.

records.paraphrase: Collection vocabulary describes head/tail structures using rdf:first and rdf:rest with rdf:nil as a terminator; the usual application convention follows the rest chain to enumerate items.

The collection vocabulary has no additional special semantic conditions beyond the existing RDF/RDFS requirements; the intended list well-formedness convention is not a baseline graph-admission condition.
records.formalization_note: Separate records cover branching, missing rest, and the derived nil self-edge witness. Non-list tails means failure of the intended structure, not absence from the semantic class rdf:List under RDFS.

records.paraphrase: The source says that collection structures other than those explicitly described, and the empty collection, are not required to exist.
records.formalization_note: This broad explanatory claim remains unmapped. The printed permutation non-entailment now has a separate record and proof. Do not interpret this prose as an exact cardinality or closure requirement on the extension of rdf:List.

records.paraphrase: An extension may impose collection syntax and interpretation conditions selecting well-formed chains whose values form an ordered sequence, including sequences containing other sequences.
Under RDFS, every rdf:first subject and every rdf:rest subject or object has type rdf:List by the existing domain/range constraints.

Two datasets are isomorphic exactly when one bijection on their nodes, triples and graphs fixes IRIs and literals, maps blank nodes to blank nodes, preserves the default graph and preserves all named pairs in both directions.
records.formalization_note: The same blank mapping applies to graph-name keys and every graph; empty named pairs must be preserved.

records.paraphrase: A present empty named graph and an absent graph name are distinct dataset structures. Forgetting empty named graphs when projecting to quads loses information; default graph, named-graph presence and quad membership together determine the dataset.
records.formalization_note: The distinction follows from the normative pair-set definition. Quad projection is an explicitly defined derived engineering abstraction. The informative note about interoperability does not require applications to treat the distinction as significant.

records.paraphrase: Simple interpretations cover the global name domains rather than a vocabulary selected for one graph; vocabulary-relative pre-interpretations are a separate construction.
records.formalization_note: Global literal coverage permits undefined denotations because IL is partial. It does not require an infinite IR. The concrete full IRI/literal domains still need an explicit binding.

records.paraphrase: Because simple interpretations cover all names, their name-mapping structure is infinite.
records.formalization_note: This concerns the full name mappings, not a requirement that IR be infinite. A natural-number injection into the abstract IRI domain now proves that the graph of IS has no finite enumeration, including a one-resource simple model. Concrete full IRI-domain correspondence remains external. Appendix B concerns finite-vocabulary pre-interpretations separately. This paragraph is a technote, non-normative under §2; the global IS/IL input-domain obligations are grounded separately in the normative table.

records.paraphrase: The RDF interpretation conditions admit a full-domain model for the base recognition set, and for larger sets under explicit sufficient compatibility hypotheses. This is a constructed consequence, not a source assertion that every datatype parameter choice is consistent.
records.formalization_note: The chosen construction excludes rdf:type, rdf:Property and rdf:List from D, allows datatype aliases and realizes every external value. The exclusions are sufficient construction hypotheses, not required namespace restrictions. Fixed built-in datatype meanings and concrete literal/IRI bindings remain external correspondence obligations.

records.paraphrase: If rdf:Property is recognized as a datatype with empty value space, no RDF interpretation exists: the rdf:type rdf:type rdf:Property axiom requires a member of that space.
records.formalization_note: A derived incompatibility of supplied datatype parameters, not a claim that the prescribed standard datatypes have this conflict. RDF-unsatisfiability then holds for every graph, including the empty graph; RDFS inherits the obstruction.

records.paraphrase: Every value in the language-string value space must have a representing language-tagged literal in any RDFS interpretation. If an abstract literal domain omits such a representative, it admits no RDFS interpretation.
records.formalization_note: Derived by combining the full recognized value-space condition with the actual literal-image condition and injectivity of value realization. This is a representation obligation for abstract parameters, not an extra axiom imposed on RDF documents or an inconsistency in the standard.

records.paraphrase: A recognized rdf:langString IRI denotes its fixed exceptional datatype; the special evaluation of tagged literals does not remove that denotation requirement.
records.formalization_note: Normative section 7 prose and the incorporated Concepts fixed-referent rule supply this obligation beyond the two literal-evaluation table rows. The earlier reconstruction omitted it; this increment corrects DConditions and the model witnesses.

records.paraphrase: Recognized IRIs identifying the same datatype have the same denotation and datatype value space, including aliases of the language-string datatype. A noncanonical alias literal uses the ordinary branch, where the language datatype has no lexical-to-value evaluation.
records.formalization_note: Datatype aliases are permitted; identification is not required to be injective. The ordinary noncanonical langString-alias behavior is a derived edge case, not an explicit source example, and remains subject to expert mapping review. No-L2V is encoded by an everywhere-undefined partial evaluator, while the actual language value space remains the normalized pair space.

records.paraphrase: The RDFS conditions admit a full-domain model under explicit sufficient compatibility and tagged-literal coverage hypotheses. For the base recognition set with aligned langString names, model existence in the current abstract interfaces is equivalent to that coverage.
records.formalization_note: Derived construction, not an assertion printed as a theorem in the source. The exclusions of schema symbols from datatype recognition are sufficient constructor choices. The existence equivalence concerns the current parameterized model class, not arbitrary graph satisfiability or certified concrete built-in datatype meanings.

records.paraphrase: Under independently existential graph satisfaction, Appendix D.1 paragraph 12 simply entails its printed singleton blank-node conclusion in paragraph 14. This checked consequence is evidence for a source-scope question, separate from the intended distinct-resource claim.
records.formalization_note: The source prints the opposite non-entailment connective. Keep the archived text intact and the question pending expert review; this derived record does not accept the printed non-entailment or declare an erratum.

records.paraphrase: RDF graphs may be infinite.
records.formalization_note: The selected paragraph also names compactness, already a separate claim. The new witness has ordinary ground syntax, no finite enumeration, and an RDFS model under explicit constructor hypotheses; it does not prove all infinite graphs satisfiable.

records.paraphrase: RDF provides no way to assert that a container contains only a fixed number of members.
records.formalization_note: Unproved expressivity claim. An infinite-member witness or arbitrarily long displayed finite prefixes alone does not establish what every possible RDF assertion can express.

records.paraphrase: The source states that adding a triple asserting a membership property of any container is always consistent.
records.formalization_note: Unproved general claim requiring explicit premise consistency, regime, datatype and fresh/existing-term scope. The new common-model prefix family is only a particular example and cannot discharge this universal wording.

records.paraphrase: There is no built-in assumption that an RDF container has only finitely many members.
records.formalization_note: A conditional RDFS witness contains a Bag with an injective family of members and a generic member extension having no finite enumeration. This choice of distinct denotations is not required in every model of the same graph.

records.paraphrase: The printed two-cell collection description does not entail the four-triple description with its two items reversed.
records.formalization_note: Each graph has its own existential blank assignment and no added type triples. The proof covers arbitrary distinct unrecognized item IRIs under explicit RDFS constructor hypotheses; no global unique-name rule is added.

records.paraphrase: RDF permits a collection description with two rdf:first values and two rdf:rest values on the same root.
records.formalization_note: The witness preserves the printed four-edge shape and proves its heads and tails have distinct semantic values. Under RDFS every tail is still of type rdf:List; this does not establish intended chain well-formedness.

records.paraphrase: A collection description can omit a rdf:rest value; first-edge information does not require a rest-edge witness.
records.formalization_note: The countermodel makes rdf:rest globally empty and refutes even a wholly existential rest-edge conclusion. Additional premises may change this result.

records.paraphrase: In the familiar collection convention, rdf:nil marks termination and can be thought of as the empty collection.
records.formalization_note: Unmapped application convention. Its normative rdf:List type is separately represented. No no-outgoing-edge, zero-cardinality or particular set-theoretic-object condition is imposed by this prose.

records.paraphrase: Baseline RDFS permits a model in which rdf:nil has both an rdf:first edge and an rdf:rest edge to itself.
records.formalization_note: Derived conditional witness, not an explicitly printed D.3 assertion. This separates the empty-collection convention from outgoing-edge prohibition and acyclicity. The model retains all RDF/RDFS axioms.

records.paraphrase: For datatype pre-interpretations, literal-value obligations are weakened to the literals occurring in the comparison vocabulary, retaining their recognized datatype meanings.
records.formalization_note: A precise partial mapping of the sketch: reuse section 5 on vocabulary subtypes, fix recognized local IRI denotations, and impose section 7 language and ordinary evaluation only on vocabulary literals. The external datatype theory, aliases and undefined ill-typed literals remain unchanged. With all names present these conditions are proved equivalent to full DConditions. Fidelity of this chosen weakening remains under review.

records.paraphrase: Under the localized datatype conditions, a graph whose vocabulary and blank support have finite enumerations is D-satisfiable exactly when its vocabulary restriction has a weakened pre-model with at most N+B+1 active objects.
records.formalization_note: Derived precise result connected to Appendix B, not the printed multiplicative bound. The reverse direction constructs a full D-model from absence of ill-typed occurring literals; it does not complete the same pre-interpretation or preserve other graph truths. Entailment equivalence remains open.

records.paraphrase: The datatype case of Appendix B claims that a pre-interpretation can be extended to a full interpretation of the appropriate kind while preserving the relevant triple truth values, within the sketch of unchanged entailments.
records.formalization_note: A full D-interpretation is now constructed on U+Value, preserving local name values, all generalized triple/graph truth under the same embedded assignment, and ordinary graph satisfaction in both directions. A checked abstract custom-datatype example shows that the current weakened conditions do not suffice for generalized satisfaction/entailment equivalence: an omitted literal forces a local property-only referent into the full resource universe, enabling a predicate-blank witness. The scope of the informative sketch requires expert review; this is not an adopted source erratum.

records.paraphrase: Under the localized datatype conditions, D-entailment to an ordinary RDF conclusion is equivalent to truth preservation in all weakened pre-interpretations with the N+B+1 active-domain bound.
records.formalization_note: The premise may be generalized and the two graphs may use different blank domains. V covers both vocabularies, including datatype IRIs; the enumerated blank support covers the premise. The proof combines full completion with the previous countermodel compression. The conclusion remains an ordinary Graph, the bound is N+B+1 rather than the printed product, and quantification over bounded models is not an implemented decision procedure.
